#10068. Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU

As part of our broader announcements for PyTorch today, we are excited to launch native PyTorch backends for vLLM (developed in partnership with Inferact) and SGLang (developed in partnership with RadixArk).

For years, TPUs have powered large-scale AI workloads with high performance and efficiency. With the rise of agentic and multimodal workloads, serving efficiently is more important than ever. Both engines already run on TPU through JAX-based backends, but we kept hearing from developers that they wanted to customize and debug their serving stack in PyTorch.

So we started in earnest on TorchTPU, which runs PyTorch natively on TPU. We then built new vLLM and SGLang engines on top of it.

Our goal is for the PyTorch community to bring models to TPU and make them fast using the tools developers are already familiar with. The engines come with optimized, production-ready serving features and custom Pallas kernels.

Serving at scale requires co-design across every layer of the technology stack, from silicon to compilers to orchestration. Today's launch of new inference engines is at the central part of an integrated, open TPU ecosystem.

TorchTPU makes the TPU a native PyTorch device. Tensors are managed as standard PyTorch tensors on a tpu device with no wrapper types, code runs eagerly or compiles via torch.compile using XLA, and collectives go through torch.distributed.

Because each device runs its own PyTorch process, both engines keep each framework’s worker model, scheduler, KV cache manager, API server and so forth, with TPU implementations underneath.

Most models use the standard upstream PyTorch model definitions in both engines, with TPU-specific optimizations in kernels and layer implementations. Custom kernels written in Pallas are called directly from PyTorch as custom operators inside the compiled graph. This platform-plugin design reuses as much of each framework as possible while letting TPU optimizations move at their own pace.

Both engines are built for the full range of production workloads.

Agentic workloads in particular demand several of these features simultaneously. Because agents repeatedly resend expanding multi-turn conversations, serving them efficiently requires finding the cached prefix instead of recomputing it. Both engines keep reusable prefixes in HBM and, with host offload turned on, automatically move older prefixes to host memory as a second tier.

Two of these features move the KV cache away from the device that computed it. Disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on separate TPU hosts, so each request's KV cache has to travel from the prefill host to the decode host.Tiered KV offload moves the part of the KV cache that no longer fits in HBM to the host's DRAM and secondary storage with Google Cloud Managed Lustre, and brings it back when a later request reuses the prefix. Either way, the transfer has to overlap computation or it adds directly to latency.

Both engines use TPU Sync for this. It is an open-source C++ library for KV cache transfer and management on TPU. It reads the device buffers behind PyTorch tensors directly, so a transfer needs no extra staging copy on the host, and it runs transfers on its own threads outside Python while prefill and decode continue. vLLM-TorchTPU exposes it through vLLM's KV connector interface. SGLang-TorchTPU uses it as a disaggregation transfer backend and as the I/O backend for HiCache.

Both engines are already running at scale in production with preview customers. To provide transparent, reproducible proof of our performance, we benchmark in public through the community-standard SemiAnalysis InferenceX project.

Building on our initial submission of Qwen 3.5 on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), our engineering teams have further optimized the stack, bringing the lowest cost per million tokens overall to an industry leading 2.01 cents. Alongside these improvements, we have also published new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance results to AgentX, the project's dedicated track for evaluating agentic long-context and multi-turn workloads. Ironwood TPU leads across most of the Pareto frontier. We look forward to continuously updating our public performance profiles as we bring more models and configurations to the leaderboard.

We did not build these backends in a vacuum. By embracing PyTorch and working directly with open-source project maintainers, we ensure these engines remain upstream-aligned and community-first:

This partnership is bringing SGLang's stellar team to build for TPU, delivering an engine that is already running in production at Meta and battle-tested at scale across demanding real-world scenarios.

Together, we integrated a high-performance Pallas megakernel for the 2.8T-parameter Kimi K3 model that runs the entire decode step as one kernel, serving more than 700 tokens per second to a single user on Ironwood TPU. Building on this work, Inferact recently led our first preliminary AgentX submission for Kimi K3 on the vLLM-TorchTPU stack. This initial milestone already demonstrates exceptional performance per TCO in ultra-high-interactivity workloads, and the rapid increase in the maturity of the vLLM and PyTorch ecosystem on TPU for doing new frontier OSS models bring-up, with follow-up submissions set to unlock even greater efficiency through larger scale prefill/decode disaggregation.

To foster continuous open-source contribution, vLLM is also launching a first-of-its-kind community contribution TPU capacity pool to provide free TPU compute to developers who actively contribute to the vLLM engine.

As the models get larger, we are evolving both engines to make large-scale TPU inference deployments performant and efficient. The major features for production-grade agentic workloads are already supported. More performance optimizations and advanced features are under way – open a Github issue to request collaboration on yours!

Across the two engines, most of the popular open model families are supported, including Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, GPT-OSS, Gemma and more. The team is investing in making more models available to run natively on TPUs, including Day 0 support for new open models. We also want to give the community the tools and TPU capacity to tune performance for their own workloads and configurations.

vLLM-JAX and SGLang-JAX remain important projects. Both will continue to be maintained, supported, and available for the community to use and adapt.

#10066. Which MCM Has the Best Revshare? A Developer’s Guide to Evaluating Ad Partners

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

An ad partner’s revenue share looks easy to compare: keeping 90% sounds better than keeping 80%. But the percentage does not tell a developer what will happen when the integration reaches production. Extra JavaScript, unstable ad slots, opaque reporting, and difficult rollbacks can change the value of an apparently attractive deal.

For teams maintaining an advertising-funded website, choosing a Multiple Customer Management (MCM) partner is partly an engineering decision. The integration affects page templates, consent handling, third-party requests, account access, and monitoring. Those changes deserve the same scrutiny as a new analytics SDK or payment integration.

This guide explains how to compare revenue shares on a consistent basis, review integration requirements, and test an ad setup without sacrificing usability. The goal is a repeatable evaluation process, rather than a universal winner.

Google Ad Manager’s MCM system lets a parent publisher manage a child publisher’s account or delegated inventory. The commercial agreement defines the partner’s services and compensation. Before comparing offers, ask which revenue streams the quoted percentage covers and whether the reporting figure is before or after that fee.

Use three separate lines in your evaluation spreadsheet:

Revenue base: record the amount to which the partner’s percentage applies. Advertiser spending, exchange-reported revenue, and publisher earnings are different figures. Do not treat them as interchangeable.

Partner compensation: identify the percentage, fixed charges, and any optional services. Ask whether the same terms apply to every demand source and ad format.

Adjustments: distinguish estimated revenue from finalized earnings, including invalid-traffic deductions and other corrections. Document when adjustments appear and which party bears them.

A common mistake is applying the partner fee twice because a dashboard already displays net revenue. Label each exported metric before using it in a comparison.

The two delegation models have different implications for access, reporting, and payments. Google’s documentation is the starting point for checking the proposed setup.

Manage Account gives the parent edit access within the child’s account while the child retains access and permissions. Payment facilitation can allocate eligible earnings from the child’s primary Ad Exchange account, but it does not automatically cover every third-party revenue stream. Confirm the invitation’s payment percentage and the separate commercial agreement.

Manage Inventory lets the parent manage delegated inventory in its own account, without access to the child account. Reporting for that inventory sits in the parent account. Google pays the parent for the relevant inventory, and the parent pays the child according to their agreement. Ask how you will obtain reports and reconcile payments.

Before implementation, document who can change tags, ad units, consent settings, and demand configuration. Agree on access for debugging and exporting historical data. A developer should be able to trace a production request to its configuration owner.

Use this table as a request-for-information checklist. It does not rank providers or assert that any named service supports a particular implementation. Obtain current terms and technical documentation for the product you are considering.

Apply the same standards to every proposal. The following examples show what a developer should ask during evaluation; each question is relevant across providers.

MonetizeMore offers publisher monetization products, including PubGuru and Traffic Cop. When evaluating its proposal, connect the commercial discussion to concrete integration questions: which scripts will load, who owns the configuration, and how will reported earnings be reconciled?

Request a sample report showing the revenue base, partner fee, and deductions as separate fields. Check whether the proposed plan includes every service shown in the sales demonstration.

Ask for a written ownership map covering Ad Manager access, tag deployment, configuration changes, and incident response. Identify who can restore the previous setup if delivery fails.

During a trial, compare representative templates and devices. Record script requests and main-thread activity alongside net revenue, using the same measurement definitions for the existing setup.

Decision criterion: choose on measured results and documented responsibilities, rather than assuming that a quoted split predicts final earnings.

For any proposal involving a header-bidding wrapper, including one from Setupad, ask how the wrapper fits into your existing page lifecycle.

Review bidder configuration, auction timeouts, and when the ad server receives targeting information. A missing bid and an unfilled ad slot are different problems.

Check whether your team can inspect the active configuration and reproduce an issue on a test page. Agree on who approves changes to bidders or timeout values.

Measure the complete sequence: consent readiness, auction start, bid responses, ad request, and rendering. Avoid attributing every delay to the same component.

Decision criterion: the implementation should be observable enough to explain failures, with commercial terms verified separately.

When assessing Publisher Collective or another managed partner, establish how the proposed setup could be tested on a limited, agreed scope.

Ask whether rollout can be restricted to selected templates or an eligible traffic cohort. Do not assume partial testing is available until the partner confirms it.

Record device, geography, page type, and consent state so differences in traffic mix do not masquerade as a revenue improvement.

Keep a dated deployment log connecting each configuration version with the reporting period.

Decision criterion: a measured comparison should separate implementation changes from changes in audience or demand.

A proposal from AdPushup or another optimization provider may involve changes to ad placement. Review the actual proposed changes with both design and engineering.

Check spacing, responsive behavior, keyboard navigation, and whether sticky placements obscure content or controls.

Reserve space for expected ad dimensions and test what happens when no ad is returned.

Compare layout stability before and after the change.

Decision criterion: additional earnings should be assessed alongside usability and performance, with explicit acceptance criteria.

For an Ezoic proposal, as for any managed platform, start with the exact integration method offered to your site.

List required changes to scripts, plugins, caching, DNS, or delivery infrastructure, if any. Do not assume that every deployment uses the same method.

Test interactions with your consent manager, content security policy, caching rules, and existing analytics.

Document how to remove the integration and restore the prior configuration.

Decision criterion: the operational cost should be visible before the first production rollout.

When reviewing a Monumetric proposal, establish which implementation work belongs to your team and which belongs to the provider.

Ask who creates ad slots, updates templates, and validates responsive sizes.

Request a support escalation process with the diagnostic information required for an incident: URL, timestamp, device, consent state, and affected slot.

Confirm onboarding costs and payment terms in writing.

Decision criterion: routine changes and production failures should have a clear owner.

Chrome DevTools helps trace third-party requests in the Network panel and investigate long tasks in the Performance panel. Capture a baseline before deployment, then repeat the same navigation and interaction sequence after deployment. Use comparable device and network settings.

Google Publisher Console helps investigate Google Publisher Tag ad slots and delivery issues. For a Prebid-based setup, use Prebid’s debugging tools to inspect the auction path. These tools answer different questions: whether the auction behaved as expected and whether the ad server delivered the requested slot.

PageSpeed Insights provides performance diagnostics; distinguish its lab results from available field data. Add web-vitals to your own monitoring when you need measurements associated with a deployment or cohort. Track LCP, INP, and CLS alongside revenue instead of treating a single Lighthouse score as the complete user experience.

Reserve responsive space for ad slots before content arrives, and investigate shifts when empty slots collapse. SitePoint’s guide to web performance optimization explains related techniques for loading JavaScript, reducing layout work, and managing long tasks.

With the same traffic volume, revenue definition, and deduction rate, the break-even increase in pre-partner revenue is: (current publisher share ÷ new publisher share) − 1. Express shares consistently as fractions or percentages. The table below shows the required lift; it is not a forecast these thresholds only describe the arithmetic. Different ad density, audience mix, deduction rates, or reporting bases can invalidate the comparison. Normalize to the same denominator, such as revenue per thousand pageviews, and compare matched periods or properly assigned concurrent cohorts.

Assume two hypothetical setups each receive one million pageviews. Here, RPM means revenue per thousand pageviews before the partner fee. For this simplified example, deductions reduce that revenue before the publisher share is applied.

Partner A: $10 pre-partner RPM × 1,000 groups of pageviews × 0.90 after deductions × 0.90 publisher share = $8,100 net revenue.

Partner B: $12 pre-partner RPM × 1,000 groups of pageviews × 0.98 after deductions × 0.80 publisher share = $9,408 net revenue.

The difference is $1,308 for the period despite Partner B’s lower share. These are illustrative inputs, not provider performance claims. Faster payment improves cash-flow timing; it does not, by itself, increase the revenue earned.

Use Playwright with mocked responses or test creatives in a controlled environment to check slow loading, empty slots, blocked scripts, and navigation between routes. Verify that the page remains usable when the ad system fails. Automated tests should not click live advertisements or generate artificial monetized traffic.

Separate unit tests for configuration logic, integration tests for component boundaries, and browser tests for user-visible behavior. SitePoint’s explanation of unit, functional, and integration testing provides a useful foundation. Define rollback criteria before launch, keep the control configuration available, and review finalized revenue alongside performance data before expanding the deployment.

There is no universal answer from the percentage alone. Compare current written offers using the same revenue base, then evaluate finalized net earnings, performance, access, and implementation effort.

Not necessarily. Reports may differ in timezone, currency, transaction coverage, fee treatment, and finalization date. Reconcile those definitions before treating a discrepancy as an integration bug.

Ask how renewals, volume tiers, optional services, and rate changes are handled. Record the applicable terms with the configuration and reporting period used for your evaluation.

No. If deductions and the revenue base are otherwise comparable, an 80% share needs 12.5% more pre-partner revenue to match a 90% share. Measure whether that lift exists rather than assuming it.

Do not treat any protection claim as a guarantee. Ask how suspected invalid traffic is handled, what evidence is available, and how later adjustments are reflected in your reports and payments.

Choose the setup that produces verifiable net value while meeting the site’s performance and operational requirements. A good evaluation leaves your team with reproducible measurements, understandable reports, and a practical rollback plan—not just a favorable percentage.

#10062. WordPress.com Student Plan

So happy to see WordPress.com offering a pricing tier aimed at students that gives them free hosting for a year:

WordPress.com offers the Student plan free, so cost is never a barrier to learning web skills. The goal is for students of any subject to create and share their thoughts and work online, and to own their online presence from the start.

I also think it’s way overdue. As someone who teaches beginning web development, I find that building a WordPress site makes for a great final project to demonstrate the myriad skills covered over the course of a semester — HTML, CSS, design, hosting, etc. Hosting those projects has always been a roadblock though.

I’ve tried several othered things over the years: Shared hosting plans (which sets me back financially), WPSandox.io (gone bye-bye though there are alternatives), WordPress Playground (saving and sharing work is complicated), sponsored hosting (it’s a hard sell on a semester-by-semester basis), and on and on.

A student plan with a year-long leash straight from the source is the perfect solution. You might think that WordPress.com is too point-and-click compared to a self-hosted WordPress.org site, but dot-com offers all the same developer affordances for directly touching code these days.

It’s worth noting that the deal is only good for .blog and .art domains. Not a deal-breaker whatsoever when it comes to educational purposes. You can always point it elsewhere down the road if you want to spend a few bucks.

I do not agree. I think it an accident waiting to happen. Read my blog post here:

https://www.usecue.com/blog/wordpress-com-student-plan/

I read your post (nicely written!) but didn’t exactly see an explanation for why a student plan is a disaster waiting to happen.

Your core concerns appear to be: (1) limited development capability, and (2) security.

(1) The student plan still allows learners to touch code as you can any self-hosted WordPress site, complete with developer tools and access. I’ve said it in this post, but I’ve taught the core tenants of web fundamentals for years. It’s not about learning WordPress, but using WordPress as a platform for demonstrating those fundamentals. And if learners are capable of touching the code — as they can — then it’s capable of demonstrating retained learning objectives.

(2) WordPress is only singled out by those concerned about security because it’s the largest and most adopted CMS, by far. Every platform (minus static generators, I suppose) carry the same risks. WordPress aggressively releases security updates and I think it’s great that WordPress.com handles the updating overhead for users.

And I’m less concerned about plugin vulnerabilities as a whole, because the final project for my course does not rely on them. The project is designed to assess core web fundamentals rather than extending a CMS.

But that’s my course, specifically. It’s totally valid if you are teaching for different learning outcomes that would validate your concerns.

#10060. CSS Navigation Matching, Early Days

Really like the intent here. Apply a style when someone navigates from one specific page to another. The idea being it’d make the sources for cross-document view transitions declarative in CSS rather than managing that stuff in JavaScript.

Bramus has a hypothetical example as this feature is fleshed out:

That’s for when we know the exact pages we’re navigating from and to. There’s URL pattern matching as well for the times we don’t:

There are additional ways to define the @location besides the pathname and url-pattern descriptors. Like maybe you’re trying to match a hash-ed URL instead, or a specific port or hostname. Apparently there’s protocol and search too, but honestly, I’d have to see examples and use cases to understand when to use one descriptor over another.

OK, so then we have a way to query the @navigation between locations using the custom idents registered in the @location. If the navigation matches the two points of navigation, then bingo.

Pretty clean from and to conditions there where they’re connected by an and keyword.

Another way to write it that’s a tad cleaner:

Or, hey, we can fire this off when there is not a match:

There’s also an at keyword to connect locations. The spec draft is vague on this at the moment, but Bramus demonstrates it like this:

I’ve gotta wrap my head around that. The way I read it, it says, “when you’re navigating between --home and --detail and you’re starting ‘at’ --home, select this element and give it this view transition name.” In other words, it happens at the very, very beginning (or end, I suppose) of the navigation between pages rather than when it’s in progress. I think. Please correct me.

And what about that :nav-source pseudo (which may be renamed to :navigation-source)? Again, gotta wrap my head around it all. But if I am understanding right, that’s to match the specific element that triggers the transition. It’s the source of the navigation, be it a link, image, div, or whatever element. I didn’t see anything in the spec draft about a corresponding pseudo that matches the element on the other side of the transition — say, :target? — but perhaps there’s no clear use case for it.

Speaking of pseudos, the spec defines another one called :link-to() that applies styles to a linked element that targets a certain location. Straight from the spec:

…which I imagine matches an element in HTML like:

…which I think is a lot like styling links based on their targeted destination? Maybe it’s more a DX convenience when there’s already a declared location?

One thing I’m already not liking is that I doubt these features would work for a site like CSS-Tricks that has such a flat URL structure. Most of our URLs are a single level deep. So, if I want to match between a specific page (/about) and any article (/article-url) there’s no way to distinguish that route. But maybe that says something about the way URLs are designed around here and they should have more structure. That’s not a trivial change though.

My friend Lee Meyer suggests that perhaps it would be possible to append a a parameter like ?blog on URL to gain URL pattern matching superpowers.

Oh, and while I’m thinking of it, I could see a possible use case where you’d want to apply certain styles when navigating from one specific page to another. Like, maybe you’re navigating between the homepage and an About page and want to style elements on the destination page based on where you’re coming from. Playing off the earlier example from Bramus:

I dunno. Seems like there could be security issues with that?

And Preethi chimed in on the CSS-Tricks Slack channel with what I think is insightful feedback:

It would’ve been great if we had an at-rule for all data infrastructures, similar to @property for all property-value pairs, with configurations valid as per type. We could’ve used it instead of @color-profile, @position-try, and now @location.

So true when there’s so many new rules to learn these days. Anything that lowers the learning curve is certainly worth considering.

You’ll want to peruse the spec draft for yourself to get deeper into the nitty-gritty of things like navigating based on navigation “type” (e.g., back, forward, reload) and navigation “phases” (e.g., loading, ready, committed).

It’s a lot to take in. But so are view transitions as a whole.

#10058. Resolved: CSS Class Prefix Selector

Just looking at what Bramus shared the other day:

First off, if you don’t follow Bramus, where have you been?! Jokes aside, his job is to be first-in-line on new features like this — especially as it pertains to Chrome — so it’s worth keeping tabs on his RSS and/or social.

It’s not a new proposal. Lea posted it back in 2024 and has advocated for it the whole while. As Bramus mentions in his post, what’s new is that the proposal was formally adopted and, as of three days ago, it has been added to the Selectors Level 5 spec draft. So, chances are that we’ll see it formally adopted at some point and implemented somewhere even sooner.

I really like the ergonomics of it. Existing substring selectors — class^="prefix" and class=*" prefix" — are verbose and defintely less readable than a simple .prefix-*.

And it’s not like [data-attribute] selectors that require not only an extra step touching HTML but still added verbosity.

But something makes me wince at the idea. I can’t quite put my finger on it. Perhaps it’s redundancy as in, we can already do this with existing selectors? Bramus cites performance issues with existing substring selectors as a primary reason we need this. But Brian Kardell’s reply resonates with me:

Yeah, I guess if we have a very specific case we can optimize it more than a general one, but I'm not seeing how this is a lot more specific than the version above which almost exists today. Feels like if we could optimize this we could optimize that. I'd be curious how it is optimized.

Then again, I do like how we extended color functions for brevity, like:

And it’s backwards-compatible, so no real harm if you continue to use the “old” way. It’s not like substring selectors don’t have other use cases and become totally obsolete. But maybe that’s it: this isn’t an “upgrade” of something we already have, but a new thing that isn’t progressive enhancement out of the gate. We’d have to @support it until it becomes a Baseline feature:

…which may or may not be a long wait. But we don’t know. And if ergonomics are the selling point, then we’re losing that in the wait.

Should also note that the wildcard doesn’t match other conditions or non-dashed cases:

Another worthy note is that the spec currently implies (but doesn’t explicitly state) that this has the same specificity as a class selector, (0,1,0). That’d make sense, as .prefix-* is really no different than writing .prefix-variation.

That said, I like how it might possibly look in a nested syntax:

…and Dave’s plea to support selecting web components:

Maybe I just convinced myself that I like it. Again, I dunno. Just take the added convenience and move on! Yada yada.

Only supporting it as a dashed prefix is kind of weird. I do like it as replacing attribe-starts-with, since for that to work it needs to be the first class of potentially multiple.

color: rgb(10, 20, 20 / .25) is invalid. The new syntax has spaces between the RGB components.

Furthermore, rgb(10 20 20) is different from rgb(10% 20% 20%).

The first one, rgb(10 20 20), is equivalent to #0a1414 or rgb(3.92% 7.84% 7.84%), a very dark seagreen. That is because numbers with no % in RGB are in the [0, 255] interval (so the % equivalent is 10/255*100%, 20/255*100%…).

The second one, rgb(10% 20% 20%) is equivalent to #1a3333 or rgb(26 51 51), some kind of seagreen, visibly lighter than the first.

#10056. Bringing Visual Graph Debugging to Custom Edge Compilers with Model Explorer

Model Explorer goes beyond high-level model graphs. See how Arm plugs in custom compiler IRs, verifies NPU delegation side-by-side, and maps cycle-level profiling traces directly onto your execution graph.

Machine learning models run locally on a wide range of hardware, from low-power edge devices to gaming graphics and physical AI systems. Running models efficiently on these targets requires compilation steps such as quantization, graph lowering, operator fusion, and hardware delegation.

Arm used Google AI Edge Model Explorer to give developers visibility into these pipelines. With Model Explorer's hierarchical graph visualization and plugin architecture, Arm built several open-source adapters that make edge model transformations easier to inspect.

When deploying a model to edge hardware, a framework change or operator constraint can alter the exported execution graph. Engineers often need to answer three questions:

Answering these questions by reading raw flatbuffers or text logs takes time, especially for large language models (LLMs) and neural networks. Arm needed a visual tool to inspect Arm-specific intermediate representations and hardware profiling traces.

To address these deployment challenges, Arm developed custom adapters for Google AI Edge Model Explorer to support several model formats (i.e., TOSA, VGF, and PTE), establishing a comprehensive visual workflow for on-device optimization. Using these extensions, engineering teams can validate exported pipelines, verify accelerator delegation, and pinpoint cycle-level performance bottlenecks directly on the model graph:

Arm engineers used Model Explorer to validate a PyTorch-trained Neural Super Sampling (NSS) model exported through the ExecuTorch Arm backend as a VGF file for Vulkan ML Extensions. While inspecting the VGF graph, the team found unintended TRANSPOSE operators introduced by a change in the ExecuTorch Arm backend.

Model Explorer enables users to inspect individual nodes of the model graph, such as the rescale operator depicted below, which displays the operator's attributes and SPIR-V tensor connections. This functionality assisted the Arm team in identifying and resolving the regression without requiring manual analysis of raw log files.

To optimize vision models for accelerators like the Arm Ethos-U85 NPU, Arm engineers used Model Explorer's split-pane view to compare CPU and NPU-delegated graphs side-by-side for a Ultralytics YOLO model.

The split-pane view showed the structural difference: the CPU graph displays each individual layer, while the NPU graph groups the network into a single EthosUBackend block between quantize and dequantize nodes. For partially supported models in LiteRT or ExecuTorch, this view helps identify un-delegated operators and split subgraphs.

To find latency bottlenecks on the Ethos-U NPU, Arm ran their model on their Fixed Virtual Platform (FVP) simulator and used Model Explorer's node data plugin to overlay cycle-accurate execution traces onto the graph. Color-coded heatmaps showed that a single TRANSPOSE node was the main latency bottleneck.

You can use Google AI Edge Model Explorer along with Arm's open-source adapters today to inspect and optimize your own on-device models locally via PyPI or GitHub.

Special thanks to the contributors across the Arm and Google AI Edge teams for their work on these adapters and integrations:

Product manager: Charlie Stokes (ARM), Derek Bekebrede

Designers: Ami Kubota, Ioannis Politis (ARM), Kathleen Low, Philip Watson (ARM)

Senior Sponsors: Bala Gattu (ARM), Cormac Brick, Joe Alderson (ARM), Matthias Grundmann, Sharbani Roy (ARM)

#10055. WordPress PHP-Only Block Registration

You want to build a custom WordPress block. But you don’t want to learn React, manage a build pipeline, or deal with NPM packages.

Seven and half years after blocks arrived in Core, WordPress introduces a way to build blocks without any of these things. All you need is PHP.

A traditional WordPress block needs to be registered twice. Once in PHP, and once in JavaScript.

But WordPress 7.0 introduces a new and streamlined approach, allowing you to register a block using only PHP.

Let’s use this feature to build a Hello World Block:

The block is fully functional in the block editor, and fits right in with all the other blocks:

The key addition is the 'autoRegister' => true flag in the supports section. When set, WordPress automatically generates the required JavaScript for your block based on the PHP registration. This includes the client-side registration, and the editor preview.

Attributes let users customize the block’s appearance and behavior. In traditional block development you not only need to define the attributes, but also build out the corresponding controls in the editor interface.

With PHP-only registration, all that is needed is the attributes definition during block registration:

This code registers a greeting attribute as a string, with a default value. WordPress generates the corresponding input control in the block’s Settings sidebar.

At first sight, there is a lot to like about PHP-only registered blocks. For any WordPress developer, it feels like the good old times when programming was simpler.

You might be tempted to delay learning JavaScript block development indefinitely. But the PHP-only approach has important limitations worth understanding.

The editor displays the HTML as returned by the block’s render_callback PHP function. When the block is first displayed or when the user interacts with one of its controls, the editor component requests a new PHP render from a REST API endpoint.

While blocks rendered this way integrate seamlessly into the editor, they are not part of the single page JavaScript application that powers the entire editor experience.

First, you cannot add any controls within the block preview. This means you are limited to the auto-generated controls in the Settings sidebar.

The default interaction mode with blocks is the block preview itself. Imagine that you need a testimonial block. With a JavaScript rendered block, you would build out the testimonial design, and allow editing in place.

With a PHP-rendered block you can only use the sidebar. And even here you are limited, as currently there’s no support for image uploads or multiline text.

With JavaScript, you can allow editing in the block, as well as in the sidebar. Additionally you have access to all the controls that WordPress Core uses, and can even implement your own.

But without JavaScript, you’ll always be limited to the options WordPress provides based on the registered attributes of your PHP-only block.

Secondly you cannot attach any JavaScript to markup in the block preview. Imagine you want to develop a block that pulls five related posts, and which displays them in a slider. For that you would output the markup, and then pass a DOM node to the JavaScript library which then transforms the raw markup into the desired slider interface.

This reliance on finding and manipulating DOM elements is typical for traditional JavaScript development. But with PHP-only registered blocks in the block editor, the markup is fetched asynchronously and replaced on every re-render. This makes interacting with the DOM of the block preview unreliable or impossible.

While the front end render works fine with JavaScript libraries, the editor authoring experience will not work correctly. Even if you manage to attach any event listeners on first load, these will be disconnected the moment the preview re-renders.

These limitations are caused by the architecture of this feature, and they will not change in the future.

On the initial load of the block editor, WordPress loads the post data from the database into a client-side store managed by JavaScript. Any changes that you make in the editor update this data store on the client side. But the database isn’t updated until you save the post.

PHP-only registered blocks bypass this client-side store. When a block renders, it queries the database directly. But the database might contain stale data compared to what’s currently in the editor. Even worse, the PHP-rendered block isn’t notified of changes in the client side data, so it can’t refresh when data changes.

Let’s take a practical example: Imagine you are building a block that displays a header element with the post title. When the user changes the title in the editor, your block will still show the value from the database. You would need to save the post and reload the editor for the changed title to show up in the PHP-only block.

This makes PHP-only blocks unsuitable for any block that displays data that the user can change in the editor like title, content, excerpt, features images, or attached terms.

PHP-only registered blocks render through a REST API endpoint. So the same code renders the editor preview and the front end. But there is a critical difference: the global state.

On the front end, blocks render within The Loop, which sets key global variables like $post. Template tags like the_title() or the_content() rely on these globals to know which post is displayed.

But REST APIs are stateless, and don’t rely on global state. The endpoint that renders the block editor preview accepts a post ID parameter, but the editor component does not pass it through. This means that your render callback has no way to know which post is edited.

This limits the functions that you can use in the block editor preview. Template tags or functions like get_post_meta() need to know about the post context.

This is a significant architectural limitation as of WordPress 7.0. This could be addressed by passing the post ID to the endpoint, but there are no concrete plans to change this at the time of this writing.

WordPress 7.0 supports only three attribute types: strings, numbers, and booleans. These map to four basic editor controls: text inputs, number inputs, checkboxes, and a dropdown.

This screenshot shows a block that uses all available user interface elements:

The dropdown element is the only advanced control, but it has a significant limitation: it does not support keyed arrays. This makes it impossible to have a label that differs from the stored value.

Let’s take the example of a related posts block where users can select a category. You want to display the category names in the dropdown, but store the category IDs. This isn’t possible.

Instead, you must choose between displaying names or slugs, which both are user-editable, and store that value:

Using slugs not only doesn’t look good in the interface, but this implementation will also break when renaming a category. All existing blocks referencing the old slug will not be able to pull the related posts. IDs are stabler, and would only be invalid when the category is deleted.

Beyond dropdowns, essential controls — like image uploads, rich text editors, or date pickers — are absent. This might change in future releases, but again, there are no plans for it as of yet.

It’s easy to get discouraged looking at these limitations. It is true that PHP-only registered blocks are a poor choice for building new blocks from scratch.

But I consider them to still be very valuable because there is one use case where these limitations do not matter: migrating legacy PHP code into block themes. This WordPress 7.0 feature is a real game changer when it comes to developers adopting block themes, which is still a barrier of sorts for many theme authors.

In my experience, block themes are more performant, easier to maintain, and faster to build than legacy themes. Yet many developers are still relying on classic themes. And that is not by choice, but because of existing PHP-based features.

Until now, migrating these features came up against nearly insurmountable barriers. First, the need to learn JavaScript block development, and set up an entirely new development workflow with dependency management and build pipelines. Second, the time needed to rewrite all this code in JavaScript.

PHP-only registered blocks remove both these obstacles.

In 2022, I wanted to migrate a classic theme to a block theme.

The content area and the footer were straightforward to rebuild with blocks. But the header was more complex, especially with the more limited block building features of the time.

So, rather than spending time rebuilding the header, I took the existing PHP-header, and wrapped it in a server-side rendered block.

That said, we need to be realistic. This header block was far from perfect. The block preview was not responsive, dropdowns didn’t work in the editor, and you could not edit anything.

Did it matter? Not at all. The block rendered perfectly on the front end, and the editor preview was good enough. And because of this approach, I could migrate the theme in hours instead of days.

Before PHP-only registration, building such blocks still required a solid JavaScript proficiency and build tooling. But now any PHP developer can use this migration path using the skills they already have.

PHP-only registered blocks are ideal for converting:

The blocks you create do not need to be perfect in the editor. What counts is that they render correctly on the front end. By using existing PHP code, adaptations to block themes will be minimal.

Here are a few things I’ve learned along the way as I’ve been playing with blocks registered with PHP.

There might be cases in which you want to have a different block rendering depending on whether the block is displayed in the admin, or on the front end.

Using the is_admin() function for this use case does not work, as it does not evaluate to true when the REST API endpoint generates the markup for the block editor preview.

But there is another function that we can use: wp_is_rest_endpoint(). If it returns true, it means that WordPress is generating a REST API endpoint request. But this could be any endpoint rendering posts, so we need to ensure that we’re dealing with the Block Renderer endpoint.

This shows different text and styling depending on whether the block is rendered in the editor or on the front end:

We’ve seen that WordPress out of the box does not give you access to the ID of the edited post in PHP-only registered blocks. There is a workaround though.

WordPress registers blocks in the init hook. This hook also runs on every admin page. When you edit a post, the ID of the edited post is passed as a GET argument in the URL, for example: https://css-tricks.com/wp-admin/post.php?post=5\&action=edit

This means that at the moment of the block registration, we can retrieve this ID. To pass it to the block, we use an attribute. But we do not want WordPress to add an interface element, so we set the source of the attribute to local.

This only works when editing an existing post. When a new post is created, there is no post ID passed through the URL. WordPress will create one when the post is first saved, and update the URL.

But this is done through JavaScript without triggering a new page load from the server. Meaning that the PHP won’t have an opportunity to access the post ID until a full page reload is done.

So, yeah, not the greatest approach. But it’s good enough to unblock you until WordPress Core adds a proper implementation to pass post data to PHP-only registered blocks.

There are situations in which it is difficult to achieve a decent preview in the editor. In certain situations, it’s even impossible.

Think, for example, of a newsletter form provided as a snippet of HTML and JavaScript. Due to the limitations we’ve seen, the editor preview will always look broken.

In a situation like this, you can implement a placeholder in the editor. This is a strategy that WordPress Core uses as well, as we can see for the Post Content block:

Users do not expect an exact preview in every case. Choose the best compromise between the time needed to achieve a proper block editor preview and the expected UX gain.

You can use WordPress optimized stylesheet enqueuing, which only enqueues stylesheets on the front end for the blocks present on that specific page.

The register_block_type function offers two arguments:

To add a CSS stylesheet, register it using wp_register_style() Then use the handle during block registration:

WordPress auto-generates a .wp-block-{namespace}-{block-name} class and adds it to the wrapper container of your block as part of get_block_wrapper_attributes().

If you need to add additional classes or styles, you can pass these to get_block_wrapper_attributes() in the render callback function.

It’s the best practice to use this class as the common root class for writing targeted styles. I prefer to use the Block, Element, Modifier (BEM) approach for writing block styles. It prevents my styles from clashing with styles provided by WordPress Core or other code.

A common scenario is that you will have existing CSS, and restructuring this code and the markup using BEM would be too much work. In that case I recommend using a unique prefix for these legacy classes.

If you are dealing with a website that uses a front-end framework like Bootstrap, avoid enqueuing any framework stylesheets. You need to only migrate the CSS instructions that the block needs, applying unique prefixes as described above.

There are two ways for WordPress to integrate the post editor into the admin:

WordPress started with the first approach but quickly realized that it made styling the block editor very difficult. Without an iframe, any admin styles can interfere with that styles of the block editor, including your custom blocks.

In practice, this means that your blocks can look different in the editor than they do on the front end. For simplicity you want to use the same styles across both the front end and the editor preview with minimal adjustment. And the iframed post editor allows you to do that.

As of WordPress 7.0, the post editor is iframed if all blocks in the post are Version 3 or higher. WordPress 7.1 will enforce the iframe approach independently of the blocks.

So, to simplify building blocks and prepare for the next release, I think it’s best to ensure that all blocks on your sites use the Block API Version 3.

JavaScript support for PHP-only registered blocks is limited to the front end. To add a script, you can register it, and then pass the handle to the view_script during registration:

WordPress will only enqueue this script when the block is present on the current page.

PHP-only registered blocks can use the Block Supports API, which allows opt-in to core features. Depending on the feature, the block editor will expose additional interface elements to the user. It will also add attributes to the block to store the user’s choices.

There are features that will work independently of the theme. Others need to be enabled by the theme through its theme.json file.

Here is an example enabling color customization for the text and background color:

WordPress will take care of the outputting the corresponding CSS classes and inline styles using get_block_wrapper_attributes().

Allowing users to customize the appearance is a good demonstration, but not something that you are likely to often use. So, let’s have a look at three useful options for PHP-only registered blocks.

All register blocks appear in the inserter by default. But this does not make sense for every block. Imagine, for example, that you use a block to migrate a legacy PHP feature only used in a single template.

In this scenario, you could set inserter to false to hide the block from the inserter. Hidden blocks stay fully functional.

Setting multiple to false allows the block to only be inserted once into each post. An example is the core More block.

Once a non-multiple block is inserted, the block’s icon is disabled in the inserter to prevent inserting a second instance.

Setting align to true enables all available alignment options:

The text alignments like left, center, and right are always available. Wide and full-width alignment are only enabled if the theme supports it.

WordPress handles outputting the necessary classes for the block’s design to reflect the desired alignment.

If you want to selectively enable alignments, you can specify them. The available options are left, center, right, wide, and full.

With these tips you should be able to make the most out of PHP-only registered blocks, even with the limitations in WordPress 7.0.

Remember the opening question: Was it worth waiting seven-and-a-half years for this?

For building new, feature-rich blocks, the answer is no. You need JavaScript to deliver the kinds of interactive and native-feeling editing experiences that WordPress users expect. PHP-only block registration won’t replace JavaScript-powered blocks, and nor should it.

Because it’s not what this feature is for.

PHP-only registered blocks are the solution for thousands of WordPress sites stuck with classic themes because of the high learning curve and high cost of rebuilding with JavaScript.

You can now take shortcodes, widgets, and template parts and port them to the block editor with the PHP skills you already have. No JavaScript. No build pipeline. No code duplication.

And these blocks that you build do not need to be perfect. As long as you can insert them into block content, and they render correctly on the front end, that is all that is needed.

That is the killer use case for this feature. And for that, the wait was worth it.

But beyond this feature, PHP-only registered blocks signal an important shift: WordPress Core is finally prioritizing developer experience. Even as someone who builds JavaScript-powered blocks regularly, I’ll admit that the process involves too much boilerplate code, and too much coordination between block.json, the PHP code, and the JavaScript. Which is not to mention that time spent setting up and maintaining the build pipeline.

Anything that we can do to make this process easier, or avoid it entirely, is more than welcome.

So if you have projects with legacy PHP code preventing a migration to a block theme, then WordPress 7.0 has removed your biggest obstacle.

Migrate these legacy features to blocks and unlock everything modern WordPress has to offer.

#10052. UK.gov lacks understanding of climate impact, says watchdog

Risks of changing climate and cost of transition to low-carbon energy poorly measured by government departments

Public bodies in the UK expect higher operating costs and energy charges as a result of climate changes and the transition to lower carbon energy, but few have a good picture of the risks, according to government auditors.

A new report from the National Audit Office (NAO) says some public bodies expect financial impact from the risks they identified, although bodies were often not able to cost these – even approximately.

"Bodies anticipate costs to arise from damage to assets and infrastructure, driven by physical damage from extreme weather, as well as from chronic shifts to higher temperatures and more precipitation. Bodies also expect higher maintenance and repair costs, potential asset upgrades, and transition costs. Many bodies expect increased operating costs, including energy charges. Bodies controlling significant property or infrastructure are particularly concerned with decarbonization and adaptation costs," the report stated.

His Majesty’s Treasury (HMT) has set out rules for climate-related financial disclosure in larger central government bodies' annual reports, which produced their first set of reports for the 2025-26 financial year. Other rules for disclosure have been in place since 2022.

However, the NAO found [PDF] that understanding of the risks in the impact of climate change –  increasing temperatures, higher risk of flooding, higher winds and longer droughts – was poor, as was insight into costs of moving to a low-carbon economy.

"Bodies did not articulate transition risks as well as physical risks in the strategy disclosures. In the disclosures we reviewed, while several transition risks were listed, few specifics were given, unlike physical risks, which were explained in greater detail," the report from the watchdog stated.

"The transition risks most frequently identified included the financial cost of transition, and supply chain disruption. Anticipated transition costs included the costs of: switching to lower-carbon energy sources, including investments in new technology; complying with new regulations; and of fluctuations in the price and availability of materials, water, energy and specialist skills," it added.

Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said: "UK public services will need to adapt to the impacts of climate change. Parliament needs clear information on the resilience of infrastructure, service provision and finances to climate change, and on how these risks are being managed."

"Although public bodies are still learning how best to report their most pressing climate risks, the requirement on all large central government bodies to make such disclosures from 2025-26 is an important first step. We expect this reporting to become more useful over time."

Earlier this year a report from Global Action Plan, a climate charity, claimed 84 percent of proposed datacenter developments were in areas that are already water stressed or projected to be water stressed by 2040.

Water consumption by datacenters could intensify strain on the UK’s water systems already stressed by climate change, it argued.®

#10051. MicroLighter: Syntax Highlighter

Here we go! Syntax highlighting for code blocks without the complicated markup, spans, classes, and bloated JavaScript, courtesy of Uncle Dave.

MicroLighter is pretty much straight-up CSS leaning on Custom Highlights, using the ::highlight() pseudo… which is Baseline this year!

It accomplishes exactly every we need around here at CSS-Tricks — themes, line numbers, multiple language support, semantic markup, etc. — but without the added dependencies we rely on.

Chris made a custom WordPress block years and years ago that plugs in Prism.js. There’s certainly nothing wrong with Prism. It’s robust, supports a crap-ton of languages, is also super lightweight, and plenty battled-tested. Either way, I’ll certainly be looking at integrating this into our WordPress block.

It’s not that there isn’t any JavaScript involved. It’s that less of it is needed. And it leans so hard into modern CSS that it brings things like light-dark() support and custom properties along for the ride, meaning rolling your own theme is totally doable.

Plus, it’s super modular in the sense that you can snag the things you want à la carte: specific themes, just the languages you need to support, line numbers, a web component.

Reminds me too of this clever little web font that brings syntax highlighting along for the ride. I’ve been happily using that on my personal site for a while without any fuss.

Update (August 31, 2026): I just finished adding MicroLighter to this site in place of Prism. I haven’t benchmarked performance in terms of page speed, etc., but I can say that the savings is pretty significant. Where Prism came in at 35 KB raw (9.3 KB gzipped), MicroLighter is at 13.9 KB raw (5.2 KB gzipped). Not bad at all considering there are WordPress-specific customizations that had to be baked in.

We've got lots of ways to help you connect with the greatest front-end community in all the land.

Sign up to get front-end roundups, browser updates, and exclusive content sent to your inbox bi-weekly.

Syntax highlighting for code blocks without the […] bloated JavaScript

This is an unreasonable claim, even for CSS-Tricks. Have you looked at how much weight Prism.js adds? Its scripting accounts for around 23,776 bytes of https://css-tricks.com/wp-content/themes/CSS-Tricks-19/js/min/global-concat.min.js, under 8KB gzipped. I’m actually not even certain that MicroLighter is smaller, once you include roughly the same set of languages; they’re pretty similar. If you use its touted lazy loading of grammars, it will certainly be slower.

There are, and have always been, good options that require no JavaScript; whereas this one fundamentally requires it (Custom Highlights are DOM-only, no serialisation defined or in my opinion likely to ever be defined).

Another limitation of this approach, which I reckon is important to mention, is that you are very limited in what you can style: simplifying slightly, it’s just color, background-color, text-decoration and text-shadow.

It’s very common to use font-weight: bold or font-style: italic in syntax highlighting. You can’t do that with this approach.

Well, like I said, it checks the boxes of what I’m looking for in a tool like this. It’s not that there aren’t alternatives that pack in much more features, again, like I said. I’m more interested in that MicroLighter doesn’t even touch the DOM.

#10048. animation-trigger

Experimental: Check browser support before using this in production.

The CSS animation-trigger property delays the start of a CSS animation until a specific trigger occurs. More specifically, it listens for a named trigger and controls how the animation plays or pauses in response.

This behavior has traditionally been JavaScript territory, typically with the Intersection Observer API.

Scroll-triggered animations should not be confused with scroll-driven animations. Although both rely on scroll or view timelines, they are fundamentally different concepts. We’ll get to those differences in a minute.

The animation-trigger property is defined in the Animation Triggers specification

The property accepts none, or a comma-separated list of triggers and their corresponding actions:

The “trigger” in animation-trigger can refer to either timeline-based triggers, such as scroll or view progress timelines, or event-based triggers like DOM events (e.g., a click). In this entry, we’ll mainly focus on timeline triggers. If you’re curious about event-based triggers, you can check out the official spec.

By default, trigger names have a global scope. If multiple elements define the same trigger name, the element that comes later in the cascade gets chosen. You can restrict the scope of a trigger to a specific DOM subtree with the trigger-scope property.

Some actions aren’t  or  only, meaning it’s possible to play-backwards when entering and play-forwards when exiting.

To actually use animation-trigger, you’ll typically need to set up a timeline trigger first. That controls when an animation starts based on where an element is within a timeline (like scroll or viewport position). More specifically, it activates when the element enters a defined activation range within that timeline.

To set up your timeline trigger, you’ll first define a custom  (like --fade-in) to link it to your animation-trigger , followed by a  timeline like a view() or scroll() function.

Then, you specify the  (such as contain) to dictate exactly when the trigger turns “on” inside the viewport.

You can also provide an optional  to define the outer boundary where the trigger stays active before turning “off”, though if you leave it out, the browser just defaults to your activation range.

To get a better feel for how this works, check out the timeline ranges visualizer from the Chrome team.

If you use different ranges, the active range must include the activation range; otherwise, the trigger can’t turn “on.”

While you can use all the individual longhand properties:

…you’ll almost always want to use the shorthand instead:

Unlike many CSS shorthands (like background or border), the order of values matters here, so you can’t rearrange them freely.

It’s worth noting that triggers and animations don’t have to be on the same element. You can define the timeline-trigger on a parent and apply the animation-trigger to multiple child elements. When the parent enters view, all children can animate together.

Let’s create a simple text reveal animation. We’ll use an element as the trigger point. Once you scroll past it, the animation plays and the text fades in.

First, define a timeline trigger on the trigger element:

This sets up a trigger named --trigger that activates based on scroll position. The range contain / cover means the animation is triggered when the element is fully visible in the scrollport (contain) and continues to run as long as any part of it remains visible in the scrollport (cover).

Next, we’ll apply the animation-trigger to the text you want to animate, along with the animation itself:

The cool part is that you can mix and match different animation-action values to get very different behaviors using the same trigger. Here’s a quick demo showing the same setup with different animation actions:

With scroll-driven animations, the animation’s progress is directly tied to scroll position. As you scroll, the animation scrubs forward or backward in sync with the timeline. There’s no concept of a “start” or “fire” moment.

In contrast, scroll-triggered animations are state-based rather than continuous. A trigger has a binary state and when a condition is met—such as an element entering a defined range—the trigger fires an associated action (like play, pause, or reset). Once triggered, the animation behaves like your regular CSS animations with no link to the scroll progress.

Here’s a pretty cool demo to see the differences between the two, courtesy of utlitybend:

The animation-trigger property is defined in the Animation Triggers specification, which is currently in Editor’s Drafts. That means the information can change between now and what it becomes an official Candidate Recommendation.

#10047. Broadcom denied names of cloud providers backing VMware merger challenge

EU court's confidentiality ruling clears a procedural hurdle, not the merits of CISPE's case against Commission approval

Euro cloud trade association CISPE can keep the identities of members backing its VMware merger challenge confidential from Broadcom following a ruling by the EU General Court.

Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe filed an action last year seeking to annul the European Commission's approval of Broadcom's acquisition of the cloud and virtualization giant.

CISPE believes the Commission erred in allowing the purchase to go ahead without imposing any conditions on Broadcom to protect the many European cloud providers and their customers who depend on VMware's software.

Broadcom sought access to redacted information identifying members supporting the action, arguing that it needed the information to challenge the action's admissibility. CISPE says the ruling allows the case to proceed without disclosing those identities to Broadcom.

"It is a procedural ruling on confidentiality rather than a decision on the substance of the case, but it removes the immediate obstacle to the action moving forward," a CISPE spokesperson told The Register.

CISPE argued that identifying the members, which are or have been VMware customers, would expose them to a significant risk of retaliation because of Broadcom's market power. Those members had supplied information about their commercial relationships with VMware.

As far as the case itself goes, CISPE says it warned the Commission that Broadcom would use VMware's pre-eminent position in the private cloud market to rewrite licensing terms and reshape the market in its favor.

Just a month after Broadcom's acquisition concluded in November 2023, partners were informed that VMware's channel program was to end in early 2024, and that Broadcom was also ditching the majority of VMware's Cloud Services Providers, keeping only a select few that had the largest turnover.

Despite Broadcom CEO Hock Tan publicly stating that inflating prices was not his strategy, that is what happened. AT&T says that Broadcom proposed a 1,050 percent price increase, for example. Meanwhile, nine out of ten respondents to a recent survey of VMware customers said they were considering moving to alternatives.

CISPE, which represents 48 cloud infrastructure service providers across the EU, says fewer than 20 European providers remain authorized to offer VMware-based services, down from more than a thousand.

Commenting on the latest ruling, CISPE Secretary General Francisco Mingorance declared it a good day for the organization and for the rule of law in Europe.

"The case matters even more today than when we filed it. In the three years since the European Commission waved this deal through without conditions, Broadcom has dismantled the European VMware channel," he said.

"Those excluded have until 31 March, 2027, to sell their infrastructure or their customers to a competitor chosen by Broadcom, or to close. This is the foreclosure the European Commission was warned about."

We asked CISPE what outcome it hoped to achieve, nearly three years after the acquisition closed.

"The immediate objective is to have the Commission's unconditional clearance annulled, on the basis that it failed to properly assess the effect of the acquisition on European cloud providers and the VMware channel," CISPE's spokesperson told The Register.

The Commission did impose conditions concerning interoperability with rival hardware, but CISPE argues these did not address the risks to cloud providers.

"We appreciate that it's a long shot (although there is precedent)," the spokesperson continued. "We have (along with others) also filed a competition complaint with the Directorate-General for Competition against Broadcom for its actions post-merger."

The precedent referred to is the EC approval given to the merger of Sony and BMG's music divisions in 2004, which was ruled to be not of "the requisite legal standard" two years later. The deal was subsequently reassessed and re-cleared.

"Ultimately, we want to do whatever we can to bring Broadcom to the table to negotiate and ideally end some of its most egregious practices so that European cloud providers can once again support cloud customers in a commercially fair and viable manner," the spokesperson added.

The Register asked Broadcom to comment The European Commission declined to comment on procedural matters . ®

#10045. Creating Web Widgets Using the Document Picture-in-Picture API

Firefox 151 recently shipped the Document Picture-in-Picture API. This isn’t the same thing as the (regular?) Picture-in-Picture API, which pushes videos into a resizable window that remains visible even after switching browser tabs or OS windows. No, the Document Picture-in-Picture API enables us to put anything into the window.

I guess we can think of these windows as web widgets. We can use them for floating stock tickers, live chat conversations, playlists, to-do lists, notes, spreadsheets — anything that we’d want to keep on the screen at all times.

The general idea is that we create a Document Picture-in-Picture window (DPIP window), and then we put HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into it. It’s pretty simple when you think about it, but as we explore how the Document Picture-in-Picture API works, we’re going to tackle a slightly more complex scenario that you’ll probably run into.

We’re going to clone a stock ticker from the main document into a DPIP window. This not only gives us an opportunity to talk about some relevant media queries and pseudo-classes, which we’ll use to write targeted CSS for the DPIP window, but it’s also a stark reminder that taking a HTML component out of context can break the CSS, so you’ll need to keep that in mind.

But for it to work, you’ll need to open the demo in debug mode. This is because picture-in-picture doesn’t work in nested browsing contexts such as CodePen
